options: Chemicals are added to make each fraction react
The oil is filtered through finer and finer filters
The oil is heated to a vapour, which rises up a column and condenses at different heights depending on boiling point
The oil is cooled until each fraction freezes
questions.hint: Think about boiling points and a column that is hot at the bottom.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Distillation is a physical process; no reactions are used.
B: Incorrect — The fractions are all liquids or gases, so filters can't separate them.
C: Correct — Each fraction condenses where the temperature falls below its boiling point.
D: Incorrect — It uses boiling (evaporation) and condensing, not freezing.

questions.stem: In a fractionating column, which fractions come out at the top?
options: Fractions with small molecules and low boiling points
Fractions with large molecules and high boiling points
questions.hint: The top of the column is the coolest part.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — They stay as gas until the cool top of the column.
B: Incorrect — Solids don't rise up the column.
C: Incorrect — Viscous fractions have large molecules, so they collect near the bottom.
D: Incorrect — These condense near the hot bottom.

questions.stem: Some crude oil fractions are used as feedstock for the petrochemical industry. Which of these is made from that feedstock?
questions.hint: Think of materials, not fuels.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Cotton is a natural fibre from a plant.
B: Incorrect — Steel is made from iron ore.
C: Correct — Feedstock is turned into polymers, solvents, lubricants and detergents.
D: Incorrect — Glass is made from sand, not crude oil.

questions.stem: As hydrocarbon molecules get bigger, how do their properties change?
options: Boiling point, viscosity and flammability all increase
Boiling point and viscosity increase; flammability decreases
questions.hint: Bigger molecules hold together more strongly.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Big molecules are harder to set alight, not easier.
B: Incorrect — Bigger molecules have higher boiling points.
C: Correct — Bigger molecules are harder to boil, thicker and harder to light.
D: Incorrect — All three change with molecule size.

questions.stem: Which fraction would be best for a camping gas stove that needs to light easily?
options: A fraction with very small molecules, like propane and butane
A fraction with very large molecules, like bitumen
A fraction with a very high boiling point
questions.hint: Easiest to light means most flammable.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Small molecules are the most flammable and are gases at room temperature.
B: Incorrect — Bitumen is thick and hard to light; it is used for roads.
C: Incorrect — High boiling point means big molecules, which are less flammable.
D: Incorrect — Viscous fractions have big molecules and are hard to light.

questions.stem: What are the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
questions.hint: Carbon and hydrogen both join with oxygen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Carbon monoxide comes from incomplete combustion.
B: Incorrect — Combustion makes oxides, not elements.
C: Incorrect — The hydrogen is oxidised to water.
D: Correct — Carbon is oxidised to CO₂ and hydrogen to H₂O.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of methane?
questions.hint: Balance C first, then H, then O last.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — 1 C each side, 4 H each side, 4 O each side.
B: Incorrect — H and O aren't balanced: 4 H on the left but only 2 on the right.
C: Incorrect — CO is carbon monoxide, and the oxygen doesn't balance.
D: Incorrect — That gives 6 O on the left and only 4 on the right.

questions.stem: C₃H₈ + __O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. What number balances the oxygen?
questions.hint: Count the oxygen atoms on the right, then halve it.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Right side: 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10 O atoms, so 10 ÷ 2 = 5 O₂.
B: Incorrect — 10 is the number of oxygen atoms; each O₂ has 2.
C: Incorrect — 3 + 4 = 7 counts molecules, not oxygen atoms.
D: Incorrect — 4 O₂ gives only 8 O atoms.

questions.stem: What is cracking?
options: Breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones
Joining small molecules into large ones
questions.hint: Think about the size of the molecules.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is combustion.
B: Correct — The smaller molecules make better fuels and feedstock.
C: Incorrect — That is fractional distillation.
D: Incorrect — That is polymerisation.

questions.stem: Which describes the two methods of cracking?
options: Catalytic cracking passes the vapour over a hot catalyst; steam cracking mixes the vapour with steam at a very high temperature
Both methods dissolve the hydrocarbon in acid
Both methods are done at room temperature
Catalytic cracking uses ice; steam cracking uses boiling water
questions.hint: One uses a catalyst, the other uses steam.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Both methods heat the hydrocarbons to a vapour first.
B: Incorrect — Neither method uses acid.
C: Incorrect — Cracking needs high temperatures.
D: Incorrect — Cracking needs high temperatures, not ice.

questions.stem: What happens when bromine water is shaken with an alkene?
options: It turns from orange to colourless
It turns from colourless to orange
questions.hint: This is the test for alkenes.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The bromine adds across the C=C double bond and loses its colour.
B: Incorrect — Milky is the result for carbon dioxide and limewater.
C: Incorrect — That happens with an alkane, not an alkene.
D: Incorrect — Bromine water starts orange.

questions.stem: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + ____. What is the missing product of this cracking reaction?
questions.hint: Carbon and hydrogen atoms must balance.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — 10 − 8 = 2 carbons and 22 − 18 = 4 hydrogens.
B: Incorrect — That adds the two together instead of finding the difference.
C: Incorrect — There is no oxygen in the reactant.
D: Incorrect — That gives 24 hydrogens on the right, but there are only 22 on the left.

questions.stem: Why is cracking useful?
options: It turns crude oil into a renewable resource
It removes all the carbon from fuels
It makes the molecules bigger so they burn hotter
There is more demand for small-molecule fuels than crude oil supplies, and the alkenes made can be used to make polymers
questions.hint: Think about supply and demand, and what alkenes are used for.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Cracking doesn't make crude oil renewable.
B: Incorrect — The products are still hydrocarbons.
C: Incorrect — Cracking makes molecules smaller.
D: Correct — Cracking turns less useful long chains into fuels that are in high demand.

questions.stem: What is the functional group in an alkene?
questions.hint: It is a type of bond between two carbon atoms.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Alkanes have only single bonds.
B: Incorrect — That is the functional group of carboxylic acids.
C: Correct — This is what makes alkenes reactive.
D: Incorrect — That is the functional group of alcohols.

questions.stem: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
questions.hint: Ethene is C₂H₄.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Ethene: n = 2, so 4 hydrogens.
B: Incorrect — That is the alkanes.
C: Incorrect — Ethene has 4 hydrogens, not 2.
D: Incorrect — That is the alcohols.

questions.stem: Why are alkenes described as unsaturated?
options: They have more hydrogen atoms than alkanes
They have two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons, because of the C=C bond
questions.hint: Compare them with the alkane that has the same number of carbons.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Alkenes are hydrocarbons, with no oxygen.
B: Incorrect — They have fewer.
C: Incorrect — Unsaturated is about bonding, not solubility.
D: Correct — The double bond means more atoms could still be added.

questions.stem: What is the formula of propene?
questions.hint: Prop- means 3 carbons. Use CₙH₂ₙ.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is propane, an alkane.
B: Incorrect — That is ethene.
C: Incorrect — That is butene.
D: Correct — n = 3: 2 × 3 = 6 hydrogens.

questions.stem: What is the name of the alkene C₄H₈?
questions.hint: But- means 4 carbons.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Propene has 3 carbons.
B: Incorrect — Pentene has 5 carbons.
C: Correct — 4 carbons and fits CₙH₂ₙ.
D: Incorrect — Butane is C₄H₁₀, an alkane.

questions.stem: Why do alkenes usually burn in air with a smoky flame?
options: They burn completely to carbon dioxide and water
They undergo incomplete combustion, which releases unburnt carbon (soot)
They react with nitrogen in the air
questions.hint: Think about whether there is enough oxygen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Alkenes are hydrocarbons and contain no sulfur.
B: Incorrect — Complete combustion gives a clean flame.
C: Correct — Not all the carbon is oxidised to CO₂.
D: Incorrect — The smoke is soot from incomplete combustion.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst. What is made?
questions.hint: Hydrogen adds across the double bond.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆. The alkene becomes an alkane.
B: Incorrect — Ethanol is made when ethene reacts with steam.
C: Incorrect — That is made by oxidising ethanol.
D: Incorrect — That is made by joining ethene molecules together.

questions.stem: Which substance is made when ethene reacts with steam, using a catalyst?
questions.hint: Water (H and OH) adds across the double bond.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Those are the products of combustion.
B: Correct — C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH.
C: Incorrect — That needs hydrogen, not steam.
D: Incorrect — That needs an oxidising agent.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with bromine. What type of reaction is this, and what is the product?
questions.hint: Nothing is lost: the bromine atoms join on.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Nothing is displaced: the atoms add on.
B: Incorrect — Cracking breaks large molecules up.
C: Incorrect — Bromine isn't oxygen.
D: Correct — One bromine atom adds to each carbon of the C=C bond.

questions.stem: What is the functional group in an alcohol?
questions.hint: Methanol is CH₃OH.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the carboxylic acid functional group.
B: Incorrect — That links the two parts of an ester.
C: Incorrect — That is the alkene functional group.
D: Correct — All alcohols contain the –OH group.

questions.stem: Which formula is propanol?
questions.hint: Prop- means 3 carbons, and alcohols end in –OH.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is propane, with no –OH.
B: Incorrect — That is ethanol (2 carbons).
C: Correct — 3 carbons with an –OH group.
D: Incorrect — That is propanoic acid, a carboxylic acid.

questions.stem: How is ethanol made by fermentation?
options: Yeast turns a sugar solution into ethanol and carbon dioxide
questions.hint: It uses a living microorganism.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Ethanol isn't a crude oil fraction.
B: Incorrect — That makes ethanol, but it isn't fermentation.
C: Incorrect — That doesn't make ethanol.
D: Correct — This is anaerobic respiration by yeast.

questions.stem: What conditions are needed for fermentation to make ethanol?
options: Boiling temperature with plenty of air
450 °C and 200 atmospheres with an iron catalyst
A warm temperature (about 30 °C), no air (anaerobic), and yeast in a sugar solution
Freezing temperature with a nickel catalyst
questions.hint: Yeast is alive, and the oxygen must be kept out.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Boiling would kill the yeast.
B: Incorrect — Those are Haber process conditions.
C: Correct — Too hot kills the yeast; air would let oxidation turn ethanol into ethanoic acid.
D: Incorrect — Yeast works very slowly when cold.

questions.stem: A small piece of sodium is added to ethanol. What do you see?
options: Bubbles of hydrogen gas as the sodium slowly reacts
questions.hint: It is like sodium and water, but gentler.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — No precipitate forms.
B: Correct — Alcohols react with sodium to release hydrogen.
C: Incorrect — There is no colour change.
D: Incorrect — Sodium does react with alcohols.

questions.stem: What is made when ethanol is oxidised by an oxidising agent?
questions.hint: It is why wine left open turns sour.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Oxidising an alcohol gives a carboxylic acid.
B: Incorrect — Oxidation doesn't remove water to make an alkene.
C: Incorrect — That is an ester, made from ethanol and ethanoic acid.
D: Incorrect — That is an alkane, not an oxidation product.

questions.stem: C₂H₅OH + __O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. What number balances the oxygen?
questions.hint: Count the O atoms on the right, then remember ethanol already has one.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — 2 O₂ gives only 5 O atoms on the left.
B: Incorrect — 3.5 O₂ ignores the oxygen atom already in ethanol.
C: Correct — Right: 2 × 2 + 3 = 7 O. Ethanol has 1, so 6 more are needed: 3 O₂.
D: Incorrect — 7 counts all the oxygen atoms on the right, not O₂ molecules.

questions.stem: Which is a use of alcohols such as ethanol?
questions.hint: Think about hand gels and some car fuels.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Bromine water is used for that.
B: Correct — Ethanol burns cleanly and dissolves many substances.
C: Incorrect — Fertilisers are compounds of N, P and K.
D: Incorrect — Carbon is added to iron for that.

questions.stem: What is the functional group in a carboxylic acid?
questions.hint: Ethanoic acid is CH₃COOH.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is an alkene.
B: Correct — All carboxylic acids contain –COOH.
C: Incorrect — That is an alcohol.
D: Incorrect — That is an amine group, found in amino acids.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid is added to sodium carbonate. What are the products?
options: Sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
questions.hint: Acid + carbonate always gives the same three things.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — No alcohol is made.
B: Correct — Like any acid, it reacts with a carbonate to give a salt, water and CO₂.
C: Incorrect — Carboxylic acids react with carbonates and fizz.
D: Incorrect — Hydrogen comes from acid + metal.

questions.stem: Ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid, using an acid catalyst. What is made?
questions.hint: It is a sweet-smelling compound.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — No alkene is formed.
B: Incorrect — No alkane is formed.
C: Incorrect — There is no sodium in the reactants.
D: Correct — Alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water.

questions.stem: Which formula is ethanoic acid?
questions.hint: Eth- means 2 carbons, including the one in –COOH.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is ethanol.
B: Incorrect — That is propanoic acid (3 carbons).
C: Incorrect — That is methanoic acid (1 carbon).
D: Correct — 2 carbons in total, with the –COOH group.

questions.stem: Why is ethanoic acid a weak acid?
options: It only partially ionises in water, so a solution has a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration
questions.hint: Think about how many molecules release H⁺ ions.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It has hydrogen atoms; only a few are released as H⁺.
B: Incorrect — Weak and dilute mean different things.
C: Incorrect — Full ionisation is what makes an acid strong.
D: Correct — Most of the molecules stay whole, so fewer H⁺ ions are released.

questions.stem: Which type of molecule can join together to make addition polymers?
questions.hint: They need a double bond to open up.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Noble gases are unreactive.
B: Correct — The C=C bond opens so the monomers can join.
C: Incorrect — Alkanes have no double bond.
D: Incorrect — Addition polymers are made from alkenes.

questions.stem: What is the monomer used to make poly(ethene)?
questions.hint: Look at the name inside the brackets.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Propene makes poly(propene).
B: Incorrect — Ethanol is an alcohol.
C: Incorrect — Ethane has no double bond, so it can't polymerise.
D: Correct — Many ethene molecules join to make poly(ethene).

questions.stem: In addition polymerisation, what else is made apart from the polymer?
options: Nothing: the polymer is the only product
questions.hint: Think about the word "addition".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Water is lost in condensation polymerisation.
B: Incorrect — No hydrogen is released.
C: Correct — The monomers just add together.
D: Incorrect — No CO₂ is made.

questions.stem: How does the repeating unit of an addition polymer compare with its monomer?
options: It has an extra oxygen atom
It has two fewer hydrogen atoms
It has the same atoms, but the C=C has become a C–C single bond
It is exactly the same, still with a C=C bond
questions.hint: No atoms are lost.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — No atoms are added.
B: Incorrect — No atoms are lost.
C: Correct — Only the bonding changes.
D: Incorrect — The double bond opens up to link the units.

questions.stem: Which monomer is used to make poly(propene)?
questions.hint: The name tells you.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Propanol is an alcohol.
B: Incorrect — Propane has no double bond.
C: Incorrect — Ethene makes poly(ethene).
D: Correct — Propene molecules join to make poly(propene).

questions.stem: The repeating unit of a polymer is –[CH₂–CHCl]–. What is the monomer?
questions.hint: Put the double bond back between the two carbons.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The same atoms, with C=C in place of C–C.
B: Incorrect — The monomer must contain the Cl atom.
C: Incorrect — A chlorine molecule can't make this polymer.
D: Incorrect — That has an extra hydrogen and no double bond.

questions.stem: Which is the repeating unit of poly(ethene)?
questions.hint: Same atoms as ethene, with a single C–C bond.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That has two extra hydrogens.
B: Correct — Ethene (C₂H₄) with the double bond opened.
C: Incorrect — That is poly(chloroethene).
D: Incorrect — The repeating unit has a single bond, not a double bond.

questions.stem: What is needed for condensation polymerisation?
options: A single monomer with no functional groups
Alkene monomers with a C=C bond
Monomers with two functional groups; a small molecule such as water is lost when they join
Very low temperatures to condense the monomers
questions.hint: The monomers link at both ends and lose something small.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Functional groups are needed to make the links.
B: Incorrect — That is addition polymerisation.
C: Correct — Each link releases a small molecule.
D: Incorrect — "Condensation" refers to losing a small molecule, not cooling.

questions.stem: Ethanediol (two –OH groups) reacts with hexanedioic acid (two –COOH groups). What is made?
questions.hint: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid make an ester.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The monomers join; they don't split into smaller molecules.
B: Incorrect — Poly(ethene) is an addition polymer made from ethene.
C: Incorrect — Proteins are made from amino acids.
D: Correct — Each –OH and –COOH join to make an ester link and release water.

questions.stem: What is one difference between addition and condensation polymerisation?
options: Only addition polymers are long chains
Addition makes water; condensation makes only the polymer
Addition makes only the polymer; condensation makes the polymer and a small molecule such as water
Condensation uses alkenes; addition uses diols and dicarboxylic acids
questions.hint: Count the products.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Both types make long chains.
B: Incorrect — It is the other way round.
C: Correct — That is the key difference.
D: Incorrect — It is the other way round.

questions.stem: Which two functional groups are in every amino acid?
options: An amine group (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH)
A C=C bond and an –OH group
questions.hint: One is basic, one is acidic.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is a dicarboxylic acid.
B: Correct — Two different functional groups in one molecule.
C: Incorrect — That is a diol, such as ethanediol.
D: Incorrect — Amino acids don't need a C=C bond.

questions.stem: Glycine molecules join to make a polypeptide. What small molecule is released at each link?
questions.hint: It is a condensation reaction.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The –NH₂ of one amino acid reacts with the –COOH of the next, releasing H₂O.
B: Incorrect — A small molecule is lost in condensation polymerisation.
C: Incorrect — Hydrogen gas isn't released.
D: Incorrect — No CO₂ is released.

questions.stem: How are proteins made from amino acids?
options: Only one kind of amino acid joins by addition polymerisation
Amino acids are cracked into smaller pieces
Amino acids are mixed with glucose
Different amino acids join in the same chain by condensation polymerisation
questions.hint: There is more than one kind of amino acid.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Proteins use different amino acids and condensation.
B: Incorrect — Proteins are made by joining, not breaking.
C: Incorrect — Glucose makes starch and cellulose.
D: Correct — The order of amino acids decides the protein.

questions.stem: What is the structure of DNA?
options: Two polymer chains twisted together in a double helix
A small molecule with one functional group
questions.hint: Think about a twisted ladder.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes starch or cellulose.
B: Incorrect — DNA is a molecule, not an ionic lattice.
C: Correct — Each chain is made from nucleotides.
D: Incorrect — DNA is a huge polymer.

questions.stem: What are the monomers in DNA?
questions.hint: There are four different ones.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Glucose makes starch and cellulose.
B: Correct — The order of the nucleotides carries the genetic code.
C: Incorrect — Ethene makes poly(ethene).
D: Incorrect — Amino acids make proteins.

questions.stem: Starch and cellulose are natural polymers. What is their monomer?
questions.hint: It is a sugar.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Propene makes the synthetic polymer poly(propene).
B: Correct — Both starch and cellulose are made of glucose units.
C: Incorrect — Amino acids make proteins.
D: Incorrect — Nucleotides make DNA.

questions.stem: Which of these is a naturally occurring polymer made from amino acids?
questions.hint: Found in muscle, hair and enzymes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Starch is made from glucose.
B: Incorrect — Poly(ethene) is synthetic, made from ethene.
C: Correct — Proteins are chains of amino acids.
D: Incorrect — DNA is made from nucleotides.

questions.stem: In chemistry, what is a pure substance?
options: A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance
Any substance that is safe to eat
Anything that is natural, with nothing added
questions.hint: Think about how many substances are in it.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Chemists mean only one substance is present.
B: Incorrect — Safety has nothing to do with purity.
C: Incorrect — A mixture contains more than one substance.
D: Incorrect — That is the everyday meaning, not the chemistry one.

questions.stem: A carton says "pure orange juice". Why is it not pure in the chemistry sense?
options: It is a mixture of water, sugars, acids and other substances
questions.hint: How many substances are in orange juice?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — A chemically pure substance has only one substance in it.
B: Incorrect — Pure substances can be liquids, like pure water.
C: Incorrect — Heating doesn't decide purity.
D: Incorrect — If it did, it would be pure.

questions.stem: How can melting point data show whether a substance is pure?
options: A pure substance has no melting point
A mixture always melts at exactly 100 °C
A pure substance melts at one specific temperature; a mixture melts over a range of temperatures
questions.hint: Think "sharp" versus "over a range".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It is the temperature, not the speed, that matters.
B: Incorrect — Every pure solid has a melting point.
C: Incorrect — Mixtures don't melt at a fixed temperature.
D: Correct — Impurities spread the melting out.

questions.stem: Sample A melts at exactly 122 °C. Sample B melts between 115 °C and 119 °C. What does this tell you?
options: Sample B is pure; sample A is a mixture
Sample A is pure; sample B is a mixture
questions.hint: Which one melts at a single temperature?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A pure substance melts at one temperature, like A.
B: Incorrect — B melts over a range, so it is not pure.
C: Incorrect — A melts at a single temperature, so it is pure.
D: Correct — B melts over a range, which shows it is impure.

questions.stem: What is a formulation?
options: A mixture designed as a useful product, with each part measured in a set amount
questions.hint: It is a mixture made on purpose.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A formulation is a product, not a formula.
B: Correct — The amounts are chosen so the product works as needed.
C: Incorrect — A formulation is a mixture.
D: Incorrect — Formulations are carefully designed.

questions.stem: Which of these is a formulation?
questions.hint: It is a carefully designed mixture.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Oxygen is a single element.
B: Correct — Paint mixes pigment, binder and solvent in set amounts.
C: Incorrect — Pure water is a single compound.
D: Incorrect — Pure copper is a single element.

questions.stem: Why are the amounts of each part of a medicine measured carefully?
options: So the product has exactly the properties it needs
So it melts at a single temperature
Because the amounts don't matter at all
To make it a pure substance
questions.hint: Formulations are made for a purpose.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Each part has a job, and the amount matters.
B: Incorrect — That is a test for purity, not the reason for measuring.
C: Incorrect — The amounts are what make it work.
D: Incorrect — A formulation is a mixture, not a pure substance.

questions.stem: In paper chromatography, what are the stationary phase and the mobile phase?
options: The ink is stationary; the beaker is mobile
The solvent is stationary; the paper is mobile
The paper is stationary; the solvent is mobile
questions.hint: One stays still, one moves.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The paper is the stationary phase.
B: Incorrect — The ink spots are what get separated.
C: Incorrect — The paper stays still.
D: Correct — The solvent moves up the paper and carries the substances.

questions.stem: How is the Rf value of a spot calculated?
options: Distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent
Distance moved by the substance × distance moved by the solvent
Distance moved by the solvent − distance moved by the substance
Distance moved by the solvent ÷ distance moved by the substance
questions.hint: It is always less than 1.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The spot never moves further than the solvent.
B: Incorrect — Rf is a ratio, found by dividing.
C: Incorrect — Rf is a ratio, not a difference.
D: Incorrect — This is upside down and gives a value above 1.

questions.stem: A spot moves 3.0 cm. The solvent moves 6.0 cm. What is the Rf value?
questions.hint: Spot ÷ solvent.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the difference, not the ratio.
B: Incorrect — That is 6.0 ÷ 3.0, upside down.
C: Incorrect — That multiplies the distances.
D: Correct — 3.0 ÷ 6.0 = 0.5.

questions.stem: A spot moves 2.4 cm and the solvent front moves 8.0 cm from the start line. What is the Rf value?
questions.hint: Spot ÷ solvent.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is 8.0 ÷ 2.4, upside down.
B: Incorrect — That is 8.0 − 2.4, a difference.
C: Incorrect — Check the decimal: 2.4 ÷ 8.0 = 0.3.
D: Correct — 2.4 ÷ 8.0 = 0.3.

questions.stem: Which of these Rf values is impossible?
questions.hint: Can a spot move further than the solvent?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is possible.
B: Incorrect — This is possible.
C: Correct — A spot can't move further than the solvent, so Rf can't be more than 1.
D: Incorrect — This is possible: the spot moved 80% as far as the solvent.

questions.stem: What does a pure compound show on a chromatogram?
options: A single spot, in every solvent
A spot that moves further than the solvent
questions.hint: Only one substance is present.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — One substance gives one spot.
B: Incorrect — A coloured substance leaves a spot.
C: Incorrect — No spot can move further than the solvent.
D: Incorrect — Several spots mean a mixture.

questions.stem: Why is the start line on chromatography paper drawn in pencil, not pen?
options: Pencil makes the spots move faster
Pencil doesn't dissolve in the solvent, but ink would move up the paper and mix with the spots
Pen ink would stop the solvent moving
questions.hint: What would happen to ink in the solvent?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Pencil has no effect on speed.
B: Correct — The line must stay put.
C: Incorrect — The problem is that ink separates too.
D: Incorrect — The reason is about dissolving.

questions.stem: Why do different substances move different distances up chromatography paper?
options: Spots of different colours always move the same distance
They are shared differently between the stationary and mobile phases; those more attracted to the solvent move further
The paper pushes some spots up faster
questions.hint: Think about the two phases.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Different substances usually move different distances.
B: Incorrect — Distance depends on the phases, not just mass.
C: Correct — This is how chromatography separates mixtures.
D: Incorrect — The solvent carries the substances.

questions.stem: A food colouring and a known dye, run in the same solvent, both give a spot with Rf 0.45. What can you conclude?
options: The food colouring probably contains that dye
The dye is not in the food colouring
questions.hint: Same solvent, same Rf.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — A compound has the same Rf in the same solvent.
B: Incorrect — It might still have other spots.
C: Incorrect — A matching Rf suggests it is.
D: Incorrect — An Rf of 0.45 is possible.

questions.stem: A substance has an Rf of 0.6 in water. A student uses ethanol as the solvent and gets a different Rf. Why?
options: Rf values are always the same
Rf values depend on the solvent used
The student must have calculated it wrongly
questions.hint: What changed?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They are the same only in the same solvent.
B: Correct — Each compound has a different Rf in different solvents.
C: Incorrect — Rf values really do change with solvent.
D: Incorrect — A different solvent alone changes the Rf.

questions.stem: How do you test for hydrogen?
options: Hold a burning splint at the open end of the test tube; it burns with a pop
Hold damp litmus paper in it; it turns white
Put a glowing splint in; it relights
Bubble it through limewater; it turns milky
questions.hint: Listen for a sound.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Hydrogen burns rapidly with a squeaky pop.
B: Incorrect — That is the test for chlorine.
C: Incorrect — That is the test for oxygen.
D: Incorrect — That is the test for carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How do you test for oxygen?
options: Use damp litmus paper; it is bleached
Use a burning splint; it makes a pop
Put a glowing splint into the gas; it relights
questions.hint: Oxygen helps things burn.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the test for chlorine.
B: Incorrect — That is the test for carbon dioxide.
C: Incorrect — That is the test for hydrogen.
D: Correct — Oxygen makes the splint burst back into flame.

questions.stem: How do you test for carbon dioxide?
options: Use a glowing splint; it relights
Use a burning splint; it pops
Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky (cloudy)
Use damp litmus paper; it turns white
questions.hint: Use a solution of calcium hydroxide.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the test for oxygen.
B: Incorrect — That is the test for hydrogen.
C: Correct — A white solid forms in the limewater.
D: Incorrect — That is the test for chlorine.

questions.stem: How do you test for chlorine?
options: Use a glowing splint; it relights
Hold damp litmus paper in the gas; it is bleached and turns white
Use a burning splint; it pops
Bubble it through limewater; it turns milky
questions.hint: Chlorine is used as bleach.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the test for oxygen.
B: Correct — Chlorine removes the colour.
C: Incorrect — That is the test for hydrogen.
D: Incorrect — That is the test for carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: What is limewater?
options: Water with lime juice in it
questions.hint: It contains a Group 2 metal.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is salt water.
B: Correct — CO₂ reacts with it to make insoluble calcium carbonate, which looks milky.
C: Incorrect — It has nothing to do with the fruit.
D: Incorrect — Limewater is an alkaline solution.

questions.stem: A gas makes a glowing splint burst back into flame. What is the gas?
questions.hint: Which gas helps burning?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Hydrogen gives a pop with a burning splint.
B: Incorrect — Carbon dioxide would put the splint out.
C: Incorrect — Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.
D: Correct — Relighting a glowing splint is the test for oxygen.

questions.stem: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid and gives off a gas. Which test would identify it?
options: A burning splint: the gas burns with a pop
Damp litmus paper: it is bleached
questions.hint: Acid + metal → salt + ?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The gas is hydrogen.
B: Incorrect — The gas is not oxygen.
C: Incorrect — Limewater tests for CO₂, made by acid + carbonate.
D: Incorrect — That is the test for chlorine.

questions.stem: Which gas bleaches damp litmus paper?
questions.hint: A pale green, poisonous gas.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white.
B: Incorrect — CO₂ turns limewater milky.
C: Incorrect — Hydrogen burns with a pop.
D: Incorrect — Oxygen relights a glowing splint.

questions.stem: Copper carbonate is heated and gives off a gas. Which test identifies the gas?
options: A burning splint makes a pop
questions.hint: Carbonates give off which gas?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The gas is carbon dioxide.
B: Incorrect — That would show chlorine.
C: Incorrect — That would show hydrogen.
D: Incorrect — That would show oxygen.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. A gas at the positive electrode bleaches damp litmus paper. What is the gas?
questions.hint: Think about the bleaching.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Oxygen relights a glowing splint.
B: Incorrect — There is no carbon in sodium chloride solution.
C: Correct — Only chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.
D: Incorrect — Hydrogen gives a pop with a burning splint.

questions.stem: A gas does not relight a glowing splint, but it makes a squeaky pop with a burning splint. What is it?
questions.hint: One test is negative, one is positive.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Chlorine is identified with damp litmus paper.
B: Correct — The pop with a burning splint is the hydrogen test.
C: Incorrect — Oxygen would relight the glowing splint.
D: Incorrect — CO₂ puts a burning splint out without a pop.

questions.stem: A gas puts out a burning splint and turns limewater milky. What is it?
questions.hint: Which test is the one that identifies it?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Chlorine doesn't turn limewater milky.
B: Incorrect — Oxygen would help the splint burn.
C: Correct — The milky limewater is the test for CO₂.
D: Incorrect — Hydrogen would burn with a pop.

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and a gas. How could you show the gas is oxygen?
options: Put a glowing splint into the gas and see if it relights
Hold damp litmus paper in the gas
Hold a burning splint at the mouth and listen for a pop
questions.hint: Pick the test for oxygen.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Relighting confirms oxygen.
B: Incorrect — That shows chlorine.
C: Incorrect — That shows hydrogen.
D: Incorrect — That shows carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: What colour does damp litmus paper end up after being held in chlorine?
questions.hint: Chlorine is a bleach.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Chlorine bleaches the colour; it doesn't leave it blue.
B: Incorrect — The paper is bleached, not stained green.
C: Incorrect — Milky describes limewater with CO₂.
D: Correct — The chlorine bleaches the colour away.

questions.stem: Which gas is identified using limewater?
questions.hint: It is the gas you breathe out.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Chlorine is tested with damp litmus paper.
B: Correct — CO₂ turns limewater milky.
C: Incorrect — Oxygen is tested with a glowing splint.
D: Incorrect — Hydrogen is tested with a burning splint.

questions.stem: What flame colour do lithium ions give?
questions.hint: A deep red.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is sodium.
B: Incorrect — That is potassium.
C: Incorrect — That is copper.
D: Correct — Lithium ions give a crimson flame.

questions.stem: What flame colour do potassium ions give?
questions.hint: A pale purple.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is sodium.
B: Correct — Potassium ions give a lilac flame.
C: Incorrect — That is lithium.
D: Incorrect — That is calcium.

questions.stem: A compound gives a green flame. Which metal ion does it contain?
questions.hint: It is a transition metal.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Lithium gives crimson.
B: Incorrect — Sodium gives yellow.
C: Correct — Copper ions give a green flame.
D: Incorrect — Calcium gives orange-red.

questions.stem: A compound gives an orange-red flame. Which metal ion does it contain?
questions.hint: It is a Group 2 metal.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Potassium gives lilac.
B: Incorrect — Sodium gives a strong yellow.
C: Incorrect — Copper gives green.
D: Correct — Calcium ions give an orange-red flame.

questions.stem: Why might a flame test fail to identify the metal ions in a mixture?
options: Mixtures never give a flame colour
One flame colour can mask (hide) another
Flame tests only work on gases
questions.hint: What happens when two colours are present?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They do, but the colours can mix or hide each other.
B: Correct — For example, a strong yellow can hide a weaker colour.
C: Incorrect — The flame is hot enough; the issue is masking.
D: Incorrect — They are used on solids and solutions.

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of copper(II) ions. What colour is the precipitate?
questions.hint: Copper compounds are often this colour.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is iron(III) hydroxide.
B: Incorrect — That is iron(II) hydroxide.
C: Correct — Copper(II) hydroxide is a blue precipitate.
D: Incorrect — That is aluminium, calcium or magnesium hydroxide.

questions.stem: Which pair of results with sodium hydroxide is correct?
options: Iron(II) and iron(III): both blue precipitates
Iron(II) and iron(III): both white precipitates
Iron(II): green precipitate; iron(III): brown precipitate
Iron(II): brown precipitate; iron(III): green precipitate
questions.hint: Iron(II) and iron(III) give different colours.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Blue is copper(II).
B: Incorrect — White is aluminium, calcium or magnesium.
C: Correct — These are the two iron hydroxides.
D: Incorrect — The colours are swapped.

questions.stem: A few drops of sodium hydroxide give a white precipitate. When more is added, the precipitate dissolves. Which ion is present?
questions.hint: Only one white hydroxide dissolves in excess.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.
B: Incorrect — Calcium hydroxide stays as a white precipitate.
C: Incorrect — Copper(II) gives a blue precipitate.
D: Incorrect — Magnesium hydroxide doesn't dissolve in excess.

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that does NOT dissolve in excess. Which ions could be present?
questions.hint: Rule out the one that dissolves.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would be a blue precipitate.
B: Incorrect — Aluminium hydroxide would dissolve in excess.
C: Correct — Both give white precipitates that stay in excess.
D: Incorrect — That would be a brown precipitate.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced ionic equation for making copper(II) hydroxide?
questions.hint: Cu²⁺ has a 2+ charge, so how many OH⁻ does it need?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The copper is an ion, Cu²⁺.
B: Correct — Two OH⁻ balance the 2+ charge.
C: Incorrect — The charges don't balance.
D: Incorrect — Copper(II) needs only two OH⁻.

questions.stem: How do you test a solid for carbonate ions?
options: Do a flame test; it gives a green flame
Add dilute acid and bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky
Add silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms
Add barium chloride; a white precipitate forms
questions.hint: Carbonates give off a gas with acid.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A flame test identifies metal ions.
B: Correct — The gas is carbon dioxide.
C: Incorrect — That tests for chloride ions.
D: Incorrect — That tests for sulfate ions.

questions.stem: Which reagents are used to test for halide ions?
options: Barium chloride solution with dilute hydrochloric acid
Silver nitrate solution with dilute nitric acid
questions.hint: A silver compound is involved.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That tests for sulfate ions.
B: Incorrect — That tests for metal ions.
C: Correct — Each halide gives a different coloured precipitate.
D: Incorrect — That tests for carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid are added to a solution. A cream precipitate forms. Which ion is present?
questions.hint: White, cream, yellow: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Bromide ions give a cream precipitate.
B: Incorrect — Sulfate is tested with barium chloride.
C: Incorrect — Iodide gives a yellow precipitate.
D: Incorrect — Chloride gives a white precipitate.

questions.stem: What colour precipitate do iodide ions give with silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid?
questions.hint: It goes down the group: white, cream, ...
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Blue is copper(II) hydroxide.
B: Incorrect — That is bromide.
C: Incorrect — That is chloride.
D: Correct — Iodide gives a yellow precipitate.

questions.stem: How do you test for sulfate ions?
options: Add silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid; a yellow precipitate forms
Add dilute acid and test the gas with limewater
Add sodium hydroxide; a blue precipitate forms
Add dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution; a white precipitate forms
questions.hint: A barium compound is involved.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That shows iodide ions.
B: Incorrect — That tests for carbonate ions.
C: Incorrect — That shows copper(II) ions.
D: Correct — The precipitate is barium sulfate.

questions.stem: What are the advantages of instrumental methods over the chemical tests?
options: They are accurate, sensitive and rapid
They need no training to use
questions.hint: Three words: A, S, R.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — They give reliable results quickly, even with tiny samples.
B: Incorrect — Skilled operators are needed.
C: Incorrect — A sample is always needed.
D: Incorrect — Instruments are usually expensive.

questions.stem: How does flame emission spectroscopy work?
options: The sample is dissolved and filtered
A gas is bubbled through limewater
The sample is put into a flame and the light given out goes through a spectroscope to make a line spectrum
The sample is placed on paper with a solvent
questions.hint: The light from the flame is split up.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That doesn't identify metal ions.
B: Incorrect — That is the test for carbon dioxide.
C: Correct — The lines identify the metal ions and show their concentration.
D: Incorrect — That is chromatography.

questions.stem: The line spectrum of a sample contains all the lines of the lithium reference spectrum and all the lines of the sodium reference spectrum. What does this show?
options: The sample contains only lithium ions
The sample contains no metal ions
The sample contains both lithium and sodium ions
questions.hint: Each metal ion has its own set of lines.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The sodium lines show sodium is there too.
B: Incorrect — Two sets of lines show at least two metal ions.
C: Incorrect — The lines are given out by metal ions.
D: Correct — Each set of matching lines identifies one metal ion.

questions.stem: Apart from identifying metal ions, what else can flame emission spectroscopy measure?
options: The concentration of the metal ions in a solution
questions.hint: How much is there?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — pH is measured with an indicator or pH probe.
B: Correct — The brightness of the lines depends on the concentration.
C: Incorrect — Rf comes from chromatography.
D: Incorrect — Boiling point isn't measured this way.

questions.stem: A solid gives a yellow flame. Its solution gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid. What is it?
questions.hint: Combine the two results.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Potassium gives a lilac flame.
B: Incorrect — Iodide would give a yellow precipitate.
C: Correct — Yellow flame = sodium; white precipitate = chloride.
D: Incorrect — Sulfate is tested with barium chloride, not silver nitrate.

questions.stem: A solution gives a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide and a white precipitate with dilute HCl and barium chloride. What is it?
questions.hint: Combine the two results.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Iron(III) gives a brown precipitate.
B: Incorrect — Copper(II) gives a blue precipitate.
C: Correct — Green precipitate = iron(II); white with barium chloride = sulfate.
D: Incorrect — Chloride gives no precipitate with barium chloride.

questions.stem: Roughly what is the air made of today?
questions.hint: Two gases make up almost all of it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The numbers are swapped.
B: Incorrect — Carbon dioxide is only a tiny part of the air.
C: Incorrect — Most of the air is nitrogen.
D: Correct — There are also small amounts of CO₂, water vapour and noble gases.

questions.stem: Which gases are found in the air in only small amounts?
options: Carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases
questions.hint: Not nitrogen or oxygen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These aren't normal parts of the air.
B: Correct — Together they make up only a small part of the air.
C: Incorrect — The main small amounts are CO₂, water vapour and noble gases.
D: Incorrect — These make up about 99% of the air.

questions.stem: About what fraction of the air is oxygen?
questions.hint: Oxygen is about 20%.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would be 10%.
B: Incorrect — That is nitrogen (80%).
C: Correct — 20% = 20/100 = 1/5.
D: Incorrect — That would be 50%.

questions.stem: What is the approximate ratio of nitrogen to oxygen in the air?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is oxygen to nitrogen.
B: Incorrect — 80 : 20 is 4 : 1, not 8 : 1.
C: Incorrect — There is much more nitrogen than oxygen.
D: Correct — 80 : 20 simplifies to 4 : 1.

questions.stem: For about how long has the atmosphere had much the same make-up as today?
questions.hint: Hundreds of millions of years.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the age of the Earth; the atmosphere changed a lot early on.
B: Incorrect — That is far too short.
C: Incorrect — That is far too short.
D: Correct — It has been fairly steady over that time.

questions.stem: According to one theory, what released the gases that formed the Earth's early atmosphere?
questions.hint: The early Earth was very hot and active.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Humans weren't around.
B: Incorrect — Animals evolved much later.
C: Correct — Volcanoes released gases, mainly carbon dioxide.
D: Incorrect — Plants came much later.

questions.stem: What was the Earth's early atmosphere probably like?
options: Mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen
Mainly oxygen, with little carbon dioxide
questions.hint: It may have been like Mars and Venus today.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today.
B: Incorrect — Oxygen built up much later, from photosynthesis.
C: Incorrect — It has changed a lot.
D: Incorrect — The theory says mainly carbon dioxide from volcanoes.

questions.stem: How did the oceans form?
options: Oxygen and hydrogen were made by plants
Water vapour from volcanoes condensed as the Earth cooled
questions.hint: Volcanoes released a gas that could turn to liquid.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The theory says water vapour from volcanoes.
B: Incorrect — The water came from condensing water vapour.
C: Incorrect — Plants came after the oceans.
D: Correct — The liquid water collected to form the oceans.

questions.stem: Why are scientists not sure exactly what the early atmosphere was like?
options: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old, so there is very little evidence
There is too much evidence to analyse
questions.hint: Think about how long ago it was.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Scientists have many theories.
B: Incorrect — It has changed a lot.
C: Correct — Theories have changed as new evidence is found.
D: Incorrect — The problem is too little evidence.

questions.stem: When the oceans formed, how did they help reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: The oceans froze the carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide dissolved in the water, and carbonates precipitated out to form sediments
The oceans turned carbon dioxide into oxygen
questions.hint: Think dissolving, then solids settling.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It dissolved rather than froze.
B: Correct — This locked carbon away in rocks on the sea bed.
C: Incorrect — That didn't remove carbon dioxide.
D: Incorrect — Oxygen came from photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Apart from carbon dioxide, which gas released by volcanoes slowly built up in the early atmosphere?
questions.hint: It is the main gas in the air today.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Nitrogen built up slowly; there may also have been some methane and ammonia.
B: Incorrect — Chlorine isn't part of this theory.
C: Incorrect — Oxygen came from photosynthesis, not volcanoes.
D: Incorrect — Nitrogen is the gas that built up.

questions.stem: Where did the oxygen in the atmosphere come from?
questions.hint: Living things that use light.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Photosynthesis releases oxygen.
B: Incorrect — Volcanoes released mainly carbon dioxide.
C: Incorrect — Burning uses oxygen up.
D: Incorrect — Respiration uses oxygen up.

questions.stem: About when did algae first start producing oxygen?
questions.hint: Billions of years ago.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is far too recent.
B: Incorrect — The Earth is only about 4.6 billion years old.
C: Incorrect — That is far too recent.
D: Correct — Oxygen then appeared in the atmosphere soon after.

questions.stem: Which is the word equation for photosynthesis?
questions.hint: It uses up carbon dioxide.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is respiration.
B: Correct — Light energy is needed.
C: Incorrect — Oxygen is a product, not a reactant.
D: Incorrect — Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Why could animals only evolve after plants had been around for a long time?
options: Plants raised the carbon dioxide level
Oxygen gradually rose to a level high enough for animals
questions.hint: What did the plants add to the air?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Photosynthesis lowered carbon dioxide.
B: Incorrect — The oceans came from condensed water vapour.
C: Incorrect — Nitrogen is still about 80% of the air.
D: Correct — Over about a billion years, plants built up the oxygen.

questions.stem: Which processes reduced the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere over time?
options: Photosynthesis, and forming sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels
questions.hint: Living things, then rocks and fuels.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — All three locked carbon away.
B: Incorrect — Respiration releases carbon dioxide.
C: Incorrect — Burning releases carbon dioxide.
D: Incorrect — Volcanoes released carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How did limestone form?
options: From the remains of land plants
From the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, made of calcium carbonate, building up on the sea bed
From plankton turned into a liquid
questions.hint: Think about sea creatures.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That forms coal.
B: Correct — This locked carbon away from the atmosphere.
C: Incorrect — That forms crude oil and natural gas.
D: Incorrect — That makes igneous rock.

questions.stem: How did coal form?
options: From dissolved carbon dioxide in rain
From the remains of plants that were buried and compressed over millions of years
From the shells of sea creatures
questions.hint: It is a solid fossil fuel.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Coal comes from living things.
B: Incorrect — Coal is the remains of plants.
C: Correct — The carbon in the plants was locked away in the coal.
D: Incorrect — That made limestone.

questions.stem: Which of these is a greenhouse gas?
questions.hint: There are three main ones: water vapour, carbon dioxide and one more.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas.
B: Incorrect — Oxygen isn't a greenhouse gas.
C: Incorrect — Argon isn't a greenhouse gas.
D: Incorrect — Nitrogen isn't a greenhouse gas.

questions.stem: Why is the greenhouse effect important for life on Earth?
options: It keeps the Earth warm enough to support life
questions.hint: What would Earth be like without it?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Without it, the Earth would be far too cold.
B: Incorrect — Photosynthesis produces oxygen.
C: Incorrect — Sunlight still reaches the Earth.
D: Incorrect — Greenhouse gases trap heat; they don't remove CO₂.

questions.stem: How does the greenhouse effect work?
options: Short wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through; the Earth gives out long wavelength radiation, which greenhouse gases absorb
Greenhouse gases reflect all sunlight back into space
Long wavelength radiation from the Sun is absorbed by oxygen
Greenhouse gases make heat by burning
questions.hint: Short wavelength in, long wavelength out.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The absorbed energy keeps the atmosphere warm.
B: Incorrect — That would cool the Earth.
C: Incorrect — Oxygen isn't a greenhouse gas.
D: Incorrect — They don't burn in the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Which type of radiation do greenhouse gases absorb?
options: Short wavelength radiation coming straight from the Sun
Long wavelength radiation given out by the Earth's surface
questions.hint: It is given out by the warm Earth.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Most of this passes through the atmosphere.
B: Incorrect — These are not part of the greenhouse effect.
C: Incorrect — Sound isn't radiation.
D: Correct — This is what warms the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Which two human activities increase the carbon dioxide in the air?
options: Using solar panels and wind turbines
questions.hint: Think burning and cutting down.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These mainly release methane.
B: Incorrect — These help reduce CO₂.
C: Correct — Burning releases CO₂, and fewer trees take less CO₂ in.
D: Incorrect — These don't release CO₂ when used.

questions.stem: Which two human activities increase the methane in the air?
options: Using wind turbines and solar panels
questions.hint: Think about farm animals and rubbish.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These don't release methane.
B: Correct — Cows and rotting rubbish both release methane.
C: Incorrect — Recycling doesn't release methane.
D: Incorrect — These mainly increase carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How does cutting down forests increase carbon dioxide in the air?
options: Trees release carbon dioxide when they grow
Fewer trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and burning the wood releases more
questions.hint: What do trees do with CO₂?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Growing trees take in CO₂.
B: Correct — Both effects raise the CO₂ level.
C: Incorrect — Deforestation is a major cause of rising CO₂.
D: Incorrect — The main effect is on CO₂.

questions.stem: Why is peer review important for climate research?
options: It lets the scientists change their data
Other scientists check the work before it is published, so it is more reliable
It means the media wrote about it
questions.hint: Who checks the work?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Reviewers check the data; they don't change it.
B: Correct — It helps catch mistakes and bias.
C: Incorrect — Peer review improves reliability, but no result is ever fully certain.
D: Incorrect — Media reports are not peer reviewed.

questions.stem: Why are there uncertainties in predictions about climate change?
options: Greenhouse gases have no effect on temperature
The climate is very complex and hard to model, so simplified models are used
Scientists have no data about temperature
questions.hint: Think about how complicated the climate is.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Many scientists agree that human activity is causing warming.
B: Incorrect — They do warm the Earth.
C: Correct — Simplified models can't include everything.
D: Incorrect — There is lots of data.

questions.stem: A website claims climate change isn't happening, based on one unpublished study. Why is this weak evidence?
options: It hasn't been peer reviewed, and one study may be biased or use only part of the evidence
questions.hint: Think about how the evidence was checked.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Strong evidence is peer reviewed and comes from many studies.
B: Incorrect — They might be right, but nobody has checked them yet.
C: Incorrect — One study alone is weak evidence.
D: Incorrect — The problem is the evidence, not the website itself.

questions.stem: Which of these is a possible effect of global climate change?
options: Sea levels rising, causing flooding and coastal erosion
questions.hint: Think about warmer temperatures and melting ice.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Melting ice and warming water make sea levels rise.
B: Incorrect — Climate change doesn't change the air's oxygen like that.
C: Incorrect — Climate change has no effect on the Earth's spin.
D: Incorrect — Extreme weather becomes more frequent and severe.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a likely effect of global climate change?
options: Changes in where wildlife can live
Holes appearing in the ground from the heat
Changes to food production in some regions
questions.hint: Three are real effects.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is a likely effect.
B: Incorrect — Species may move or die out.
C: Correct — This is not an effect of climate change.
D: Incorrect — Crops may fail or grow differently.

questions.stem: What is a major cause of global climate change?
options: A rise in the average global temperature
A fall in the amount of nitrogen in the air
questions.hint: Think about temperature.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That isn't the cause.
B: Incorrect — This isn't a cause of climate change.
C: Correct — Warming changes weather and climate patterns.
D: Incorrect — Nitrogen levels have stayed steady.

questions.stem: What is a carbon footprint?
options: The amount of carbon in a person's body
The total amount of greenhouse gases (mainly CO₂) given out over the full life cycle of a product, service or event
The mark left by a shoe in coal dust
The amount of oxygen a product uses
questions.hint: Think about a whole life cycle.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It measures emissions, not body carbon.
B: Correct — It includes making, using and disposing of it.
C: Incorrect — It is about greenhouse gas emissions.
D: Incorrect — It measures greenhouse gases given out.

questions.stem: Which action would reduce a carbon footprint?
options: Using renewable energy instead of fossil fuels
questions.hint: Fewer greenhouse gases given out.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That increases CO₂.
B: Incorrect — Landfill releases methane.
C: Incorrect — That releases more CO₂.
D: Correct — It means less carbon dioxide is released.

questions.stem: Why might it be hard to reduce carbon dioxide emissions?
options: Renewable energy releases more CO₂ than fossil fuels
Carbon dioxide cannot be reduced at all
Nobody knows what causes carbon dioxide emissions
New technology can be expensive, and people may not want to change their lifestyles
questions.hint: Think about cost and people.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Renewables release far less.
B: Incorrect — Emissions can be reduced.
C: Incorrect — The causes are well known.
D: Correct — Countries and people may not agree or be able to afford it.

questions.stem: What is a major source of air pollution?
questions.hint: Cars, power stations and boilers all do it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Photosynthesis releases oxygen.
B: Incorrect — Rain doesn't create pollutants.
C: Correct — Combustion releases several pollutants.
D: Incorrect — This isn't a major source of air pollution.

questions.stem: When does carbon monoxide form?
options: When a fuel burns with not enough oxygen (incomplete combustion)
When a fuel burns with plenty of oxygen
When sulfur in the fuel burns
questions.hint: Think about the amount of oxygen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That makes oxides of nitrogen.
B: Correct — Carbon is only partly oxidised.
C: Incorrect — Complete combustion makes CO₂.
D: Incorrect — That makes sulfur dioxide.

questions.stem: Where does the sulfur dioxide from burning fuels come from?
options: Sulfur impurities in the fuel react with oxygen
questions.hint: It isn't from the air.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That makes oxides of nitrogen.
B: Incorrect — That makes carbon monoxide and soot.
C: Correct — Some fuels, such as coal, contain sulfur.
D: Incorrect — There is very little sulfur in the air.

questions.stem: How are oxides of nitrogen formed in a car engine?
options: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperatures in the engine
questions.hint: The nitrogen doesn't come from the fuel.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Oxides of nitrogen contain no carbon.
B: Incorrect — The nitrogen comes from the air.
C: Incorrect — Oxides of nitrogen contain nitrogen and oxygen.
D: Correct — The engine is hot enough for nitrogen to react.

questions.stem: What is soot?
options: Solid particles of carbon from incomplete combustion
questions.hint: It is a black solid.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Water vapour is a gas.
B: Correct — Not all the carbon is turned into a gas.
C: Incorrect — Soot is a solid.
D: Incorrect — Sulfur dioxide is a gas.

questions.stem: Which two products are made when a hydrocarbon burns completely?
questions.hint: Carbon and hydrogen are both fully oxidised.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Sulfur dioxide needs sulfur in the fuel.
B: Incorrect — These come from incomplete combustion.
C: Correct — These are the products of complete combustion.
D: Incorrect — Oxides of nitrogen form from the air, not the hydrocarbon.

questions.stem: A fuel contains carbon, hydrogen and sulfur. It is burnt with a limited supply of air. Which products could form?
options: Carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, soot, water vapour and sulfur dioxide
questions.hint: Use every element, and remember there isn't enough oxygen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Sulfur dioxide forms, and limited air gives CO and soot.
B: Incorrect — The carbon and hydrogen form products too.
C: Incorrect — The elements are oxidised, not released.
D: Correct — Carbon gives CO₂, CO and C; hydrogen gives water; sulfur gives SO₂.

questions.stem: Which pollutant could NOT come from burning pure methane (CH₄) in a car engine?
questions.hint: Which element is missing from methane and from the air?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This can form from incomplete combustion.
B: Correct — Neither methane nor the air contains sulfur.
C: Incorrect — This can form if there isn't enough oxygen.
D: Incorrect — These form from nitrogen in the air at high temperatures.

questions.stem: Which pollutant comes from fuel that passes through an engine without burning?
questions.hint: They are still hydrocarbons.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That forms when the fuel does burn.
B: Incorrect — These form from nitrogen in the air.
C: Correct — Some fuel escapes without reacting.
D: Incorrect — That forms when sulfur burns.

questions.stem: Why is carbon monoxide especially dangerous?
options: It is toxic, and it is colourless and odourless, so it is hard to detect
It has a strong smell that makes people ill
It is a solid that blocks sunlight
questions.hint: Could you notice it?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — You can't see or smell it.
B: Incorrect — Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause acid rain.
C: Incorrect — It has no smell.
D: Incorrect — Carbon monoxide is a gas.

questions.stem: Which problems do sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause?
questions.hint: They dissolve in rainwater.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is caused by particulates.
B: Incorrect — They are harmful pollutants.
C: Incorrect — They don't add oxygen.
D: Correct — They form acids in rain and irritate the lungs.

questions.stem: Which problems do particulates (tiny solid particles such as soot) cause?
options: A hole in the ozone layer
questions.hint: They block sunlight and get into lungs.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — They reflect sunlight and damage the lungs.
B: Incorrect — Soot doesn't cause this; particulates cause dimming and health problems.
C: Incorrect — Acid rain is caused by SO₂ and oxides of nitrogen.
D: Incorrect — They reduce the light reaching the ground.

questions.stem: What is global dimming?
options: The Sun giving out less light
Less sunlight reaching the Earth's surface because particulates reflect it
questions.hint: Less of something reaches the ground.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The Sun hasn't changed; the particles block light.
B: Correct — Particles in the air block some sunlight.
C: Incorrect — It is about sunlight and particulates.
D: Incorrect — That traps heat; dimming reduces sunlight.

questions.stem: A town has high levels of sulfur dioxide. Which problem is most likely?
options: Acid rain damaging buildings, and people having breathing problems
questions.hint: Think lungs and rain.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Sulfur dioxide causes both.
B: Incorrect — Sulfur dioxide doesn't add oxygen.
C: Incorrect — That is caused by particulates.
D: Incorrect — That is caused by carbon monoxide.

questions.stem: Which of these is a renewable resource?
questions.hint: Renewable means it can be replaced as fast as we use it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Crude oil takes millions of years to form, so it is finite.
B: Incorrect — Metal ores are finite.
C: Incorrect — Natural gas is a finite fossil fuel.
D: Correct — New trees can be planted and grown.

questions.stem: Which of these is a finite resource?
questions.hint: It will run out.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Crops are replanted every year.
B: Incorrect — Cotton plants can be grown again.
C: Incorrect — Sheep grow new wool.
D: Correct — They can't be replaced once mined.

questions.stem: What is sustainable development?
options: Using up resources as fast as possible
Meeting the needs of people today without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
questions.hint: Think about now and the future.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — We have to use some resources to live.
B: Incorrect — That harms future generations.
C: Incorrect — Finite resources will run out.
D: Correct — Chemistry helps by improving processes and saving resources.

questions.stem: What is potable water?
options: Pure water with nothing dissolved in it
Water that is safe to drink, with low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
questions.hint: "Potable" means drinkable.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Sea water has too much salt to drink.
B: Incorrect — Potable water still has some dissolved substances.
C: Correct — It is safe, but it isn't chemically pure.
D: Incorrect — Boiling alone doesn't make water potable.

questions.stem: Why is potable water not pure water in the chemical sense?
options: It is full of harmful microbes
It contains small amounts of dissolved substances
It contains large amounts of salt
questions.hint: What else is in tap water?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It has been sterilised.
B: Correct — Pure water would contain only H₂O.
C: Incorrect — It is a liquid.
D: Incorrect — The salt level is low.

questions.stem: In the UK, what are the main steps in making fresh water potable?
options: Choose a source of fresh water, pass it through filter beds, then sterilise it
questions.hint: Pass it through something, then kill the microbes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This isn't how water is treated.
B: Incorrect — Adding salt doesn't help.
C: Correct — The filter beds remove solids; sterilising kills microbes.
D: Incorrect — That is desalination, used where fresh water is short.

questions.stem: Which of these is used to sterilise drinking water?
questions.hint: It kills microbes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Salt doesn't sterilise drinking water.
B: Incorrect — Carbon dioxide isn't used to sterilise water.
C: Incorrect — Sugar doesn't kill microbes.
D: Correct — Chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light are all used.

questions.stem: Which methods are used to desalinate sea water?
questions.hint: One uses boiling; one uses membranes.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Both remove the dissolved salts.
B: Incorrect — That separates dyes, not water from salt.
C: Incorrect — Chlorine kills microbes but doesn't remove salt.
D: Incorrect — Filtering can't remove dissolved salt.

questions.stem: Why is desalination not the main way of getting drinking water in the UK?
options: The UK has no access to the sea
It needs large amounts of energy, and the UK has plenty of fresh rainwater
questions.hint: Think about energy, and how much rain the UK gets.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The UK is surrounded by sea.
B: Incorrect — Desalination does remove the salt.
C: Incorrect — Desalinated water is safe to drink.
D: Correct — Desalination is used where fresh water is limited.

questions.stem: What is the first stage of sewage treatment?
questions.hint: Remove the big bits.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That comes after sedimentation.
B: Correct — This takes out large objects and grit.
C: Incorrect — That comes after sedimentation.
D: Incorrect — That isn't the first sewage stage.

questions.stem: In sewage treatment, what does sedimentation produce?
options: Sludge (which settles) and effluent (the liquid above)
questions.hint: Something settles; something stays on top.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Those are removed in the first stage.
B: Correct — Each is then treated in a different way.
C: Incorrect — These are sterilising agents.
D: Incorrect — Sedimentation doesn't make pure water.

questions.stem: How are the sludge and the effluent from sewage treated?
options: Sludge by anaerobic digestion; effluent by aerobic biological treatment
Sludge by aerobic treatment; effluent by anaerobic digestion
questions.hint: One without air, one with air.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Microbes break down the organic matter in both.
B: Incorrect — It is the other way round.
C: Incorrect — Salt isn't used in sewage treatment.
D: Incorrect — Distillation is used for desalination.

questions.stem: Besides organic matter and microbes, what may also need removing from industrial waste water?
questions.hint: Factories use many substances.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Oxygen isn't a pollutant in water.
B: Incorrect — Industrial waste often needs extra treatment.
C: Correct — Industrial waste can contain toxic substances.
D: Incorrect — The water is what we want to keep.

questions.stem: Which source would need the most energy to turn into potable water?
options: Sea water, because the salt must be removed by distillation or reverse osmosis
Water from a clean mountain lake
questions.hint: Which one has lots of dissolved salt?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Fresh ground water is fairly easy to treat.
B: Incorrect — This only needs filtering and sterilising.
C: Correct — Both methods use large amounts of energy.
D: Incorrect — This is fresh water and is easy to treat.

questions.stem: What is phytomining?
options: Digging up ores with large machines
Using bacteria to make solutions of metal compounds
Growing plants that absorb metal compounds, then harvesting and burning them; the ash contains the metal compounds
questions.hint: "Phyto" means plant.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Traditional mining is what phytomining avoids.
B: Incorrect — That is bioleaching.
C: Correct — Used for low-grade copper ores.
D: Incorrect — That is reduction with carbon.

questions.stem: What is bioleaching?
options: Using bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds
questions.hint: "Bio" means living.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is phytomining.
B: Correct — The metal can then be extracted from the solution.
C: Incorrect — That doesn't use living things.
D: Incorrect — That doesn't use living things.

questions.stem: Why are phytomining and bioleaching used to extract copper?
options: They work only on pure copper
High-grade copper ores are running out, and these methods avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock
They are much faster than traditional mining
questions.hint: Think about how much copper ore is left.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They are used on low-grade ores.
B: Correct — They can use low-grade ores.
C: Incorrect — They don't change copper's reactivity.
D: Incorrect — They are actually slow.

questions.stem: How can copper be obtained from a solution of copper compounds made by bioleaching?
options: Displacement using scrap iron, or electrolysis
questions.hint: Two methods: one uses a more reactive metal, one uses electricity.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The bacteria make the solution; they don't remove the copper.
B: Correct — Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it.
C: Incorrect — Silver is less reactive than copper, so it can't displace it.
D: Incorrect — The copper is dissolved, so it passes through a filter.

questions.stem: What are the four stages in a life cycle assessment (LCA)?
options: Extracting raw materials; making and packaging; using; disposal
questions.hint: From the ground to the bin.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These are changes of state.
B: Incorrect — An LCA is about environmental impact, not money.
C: Incorrect — These are ways to save resources.
D: Correct — Transport at each stage is included too.

questions.stem: Making plastic from crude oil belongs to which stage of an LCA?
questions.hint: It happens before the product is made.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Crude oil is the raw material.
B: Incorrect — This is before the product exists.
C: Incorrect — This happens at the start, not the end.
D: Incorrect — This is processing the raw material.

questions.stem: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?
options: The effects of pollutants are hard to measure, so value judgements are needed
Nothing in an LCA can be measured
LCAs are always done by computers
questions.hint: Some things are easy to measure; some aren't.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Energy and water use are easy to measure; harm from pollution isn't.
B: Incorrect — Disposal is one of the four stages.
C: Incorrect — Use of water, energy and resources can be measured.
D: Incorrect — Who does it isn't the issue.

questions.stem: How can a life cycle assessment be misused?
options: A shortened or selective LCA can be used to support a claim, such as in advertising
questions.hint: Think about adverts.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Leaving out stages can make a product look greener.
B: Incorrect — Selective LCAs can mislead.
C: Incorrect — Measuring energy is a normal part of an LCA.
D: Incorrect — That is how it should be done.

questions.stem: In an LCA comparing shopping bags, which is an advantage of paper bags over plastic bags?
options: They are made from trees, a renewable resource, and they biodegrade
They can be reused many more times
They are made from crude oil
They never need any energy to make
questions.hint: Think about the raw material and what happens at disposal.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Plastic bags come from crude oil and last a long time.
B: Incorrect — Plastic bags are usually stronger and reused more.
C: Incorrect — Plastic bags are made from crude oil.
D: Incorrect — Making paper uses a lot of energy.

questions.stem: Making bag A uses 1.5 MJ of energy and it is used once. Making bag B uses 2.5 MJ and it is used 5 times. Which uses less energy per use?
questions.hint: Divide the energy by the number of uses.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Bag A uses 1.5 MJ per use, which is more than bag B.
B: Correct — 2.5 ÷ 5 = 0.5 MJ, compared with 1.5 ÷ 1 = 1.5 MJ for bag A.
C: Incorrect — 1.5 MJ per use and 0.5 MJ per use are different.
D: Incorrect — That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: What are the three ways of reducing the use of resources?
questions.hint: Three Rs.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These aren't the three Rs.
B: Correct — All three save resources and energy and cut waste.
C: Incorrect — These aren't the three Rs.
D: Incorrect — These aren't the three Rs.

questions.stem: Why is it important to reduce the use of materials such as metals and glass?
options: They are renewable, so it doesn't matter
They come from limited raw materials, and getting them uses energy and harms the environment
They need no energy to produce
questions.hint: Where do their raw materials come from?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Making them creates waste.
B: Incorrect — Their raw materials are limited.
C: Correct — Quarrying and mining damage the landscape.
D: Incorrect — Producing them uses a lot of energy.

questions.stem: How can glass bottles be recycled?
options: Reused, or crushed and melted to make new glass products
questions.hint: Two options: use again, or remake.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Glass doesn't dissolve in water.
B: Incorrect — Glass can't be turned into metal.
C: Incorrect — Glass doesn't burn.
D: Correct — Both reduce the need for new raw materials.

questions.stem: How can scrap steel be used to reduce the use of iron ore?
options: It is turned back into iron ore
It is added to iron from the blast furnace
questions.hint: It goes into the iron-making process.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Steel isn't a fuel.
B: Incorrect — It is melted and reused, not turned into ore.
C: Incorrect — That wastes it.
D: Correct — Less new iron ore is then needed.

questions.stem: What is one environmental impact of quarrying and mining for raw materials?
options: It destroys habitats and scars the landscape
It has no impact at all
questions.hint: Think about the land.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Large amounts of rock are dug up and moved.
B: Incorrect — It usually destroys habitats.
C: Incorrect — Mining makes dust and noise.
D: Incorrect — It has large impacts.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of recycling metals?
options: It uses more ore than mining
Collecting, transporting and sorting the waste uses energy and costs money
