Recycled metals can never be melted
questions.hint: Recycling isn't free.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Recycling uses less ore.
B: Correct — It is usually still less than extracting new metal.
C: Incorrect — It reduces landfill waste.
D: Incorrect — Metals can be melted and reshaped.

questions.stem: How are metals recycled?
options: They are crushed into powder and thrown away
They are melted and recast or reformed into new products
questions.hint: Think about heat.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Metals don't dissolve in water.
B: Incorrect — That doesn't recycle them.
C: Correct — Recycling metal saves ore and energy.
D: Incorrect — Burning doesn't make new metal products.

questions.stem: What is corrosion?
options: The destruction of a material by chemical reactions with substances in its environment
questions.hint: Rusting is an example.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Polishing doesn't destroy the material.
B: Incorrect — Alloys are made by mixing metals.
C: Correct — For example, iron reacting with air and water.
D: Incorrect — Melting is a physical change.

questions.stem: What does iron need in order to rust?
questions.hint: Two things.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Air alone isn't enough.
B: Incorrect — Salt speeds rusting up, but air and water are what is needed.
C: Correct — Without either one, iron doesn't rust.
D: Incorrect — Water alone isn't enough.

questions.stem: A nail is put in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. Why doesn't it rust?
options: Boiling removed the dissolved air, and the oil stops air getting back in
Oil reacts with iron to protect it
questions.hint: What has been kept out?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The water has cooled; it is the lack of air.
B: Correct — With no air, iron can't rust.
C: Incorrect — The nail is in water.
D: Incorrect — The oil is a barrier to air.

questions.stem: Which of these prevents rusting by acting as a barrier?
options: Leaving it outside in the rain
questions.hint: It stops air and water reaching the iron.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Salt water speeds rusting.
B: Incorrect — That removes protection.
C: Incorrect — That speeds up rusting.
D: Correct — Paint coats the surface.

questions.stem: How does zinc protect iron from rusting, even if the zinc coating is scratched?
options: Zinc makes the iron into an alloy
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it reacts instead of the iron (sacrificial protection)
Zinc is less reactive than iron
questions.hint: Compare their reactivity.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The zinc is a coating.
B: Correct — The zinc corrodes first.
C: Incorrect — A less reactive metal can't protect iron this way.
D: Incorrect — It is about reactivity.

questions.stem: What is galvanising?
options: Heating iron to make it stronger
Coating iron with a layer of zinc
questions.hint: It uses zinc.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is painting.
B: Incorrect — That makes steel.
C: Incorrect — That isn't galvanising.
D: Correct — The zinc acts as a barrier and as sacrificial protection.

questions.stem: Why does aluminium not corrode much, even though it is fairly reactive?
options: A thin oxide layer forms on its surface and protects it
It is less reactive than gold
questions.hint: Something forms on its surface.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It reacts to form the oxide layer.
B: Correct — The oxide stops further reaction.
C: Incorrect — It is much more reactive than gold.
D: Incorrect — The protection is natural.

questions.stem: Which metal could be used for sacrificial protection of iron?
questions.hint: It must be more reactive than iron.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Silver is less reactive than iron.
B: Incorrect — Gold is much less reactive.
C: Incorrect — Copper is less reactive than iron.
D: Correct — Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first.

questions.stem: Bronze is an alloy of which metals?
questions.hint: Used for statues and medals.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Bronze is copper and tin.
B: Incorrect — That is brass.
C: Incorrect — That isn't bronze.
D: Incorrect — That is steel.

questions.stem: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. What is it used for?
options: Water taps, door fittings and musical instruments
questions.hint: Shiny and doesn't corrode easily.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Steel is used for that.
B: Incorrect — Fertilisers aren't made from brass.
C: Correct — Brass is hard and doesn't corrode easily.
D: Incorrect — Aluminium alloys are used for that.

questions.stem: What percentage of 18 carat gold is pure gold?
questions.hint: 24 carat is 100% gold.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75 = 75%.
B: Incorrect — Carat isn't a percentage.
C: Incorrect — That would be 24 carat.
D: Incorrect — That would be 12 carat.

questions.stem: A ring is 12 carat gold. What fraction of it is gold?
questions.hint: Compare it with 24 carat.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would be 6 carat.
B: Incorrect — That would be 24 carat.
C: Incorrect — That would be 18 carat.
D: Correct — 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5, so half is gold.

questions.stem: How do high-carbon steel and low-carbon steel compare?
options: High-carbon steel is strong but brittle; low-carbon steel is softer and easily shaped
They have exactly the same properties
High-carbon steel is soft; low-carbon steel is brittle
questions.hint: More carbon makes it harder.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The amount of carbon changes the properties.
B: Incorrect — Both are iron alloys.
C: Incorrect — Carbon content changes the properties.
D: Incorrect — It is the other way round.

questions.stem: Stainless steel contains chromium and nickel. Why is it used for cutlery?
options: It has a very low density
It is hard and resistant to corrosion
questions.hint: Think about washing up.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It is an alloy.
B: Incorrect — Aluminium alloys have low density.
C: Incorrect — It is hard.
D: Correct — It doesn't rust when wet.

questions.stem: Why are aluminium alloys used to build aircraft?
options: They melt at a low temperature
questions.hint: Aircraft need to be light.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Aircraft need light materials.
B: Incorrect — Aluminium alloys resist corrosion.
C: Correct — Light but strong materials save fuel.
D: Incorrect — That isn't the reason.

questions.stem: Soda-lime glass is made by heating which substances?
questions.hint: Three raw materials, one is sand.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That makes clay ceramics.
B: Correct — This is the most common type of glass.
C: Incorrect — Ethene makes poly(ethene).
D: Incorrect — That makes borosilicate glass.

questions.stem: Why is borosilicate glass used for oven dishes and lab glassware?
options: It melts at a higher temperature than soda-lime glass
It melts at a lower temperature
questions.hint: Compare its melting temperature with soda-lime glass.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It is a ceramic glass.
B: Correct — It can stand up to more heat.
C: Incorrect — It is made from sand and boron trioxide.
D: Incorrect — That would make it worse for heating.

questions.stem: How are clay ceramics, such as pottery and bricks, made?
options: Wet clay is shaped and then heated in a furnace
Sand is melted with sodium carbonate
questions.hint: Shape, then heat.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That makes poly(ethene).
B: Incorrect — That makes alloys.
C: Correct — The heat makes it hard.
D: Incorrect — That makes glass.

questions.stem: Low density and high density poly(ethene) are both made from ethene. Why are they different?
options: They are made using different reaction conditions and catalysts
They are made from different monomers
questions.hint: Same monomer, different ...
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The conditions change how the chains form.
B: Incorrect — Neither contains chlorine.
C: Incorrect — Both are made from ethene.
D: Incorrect — Both are polymers.

questions.stem: Why do thermosetting polymers not melt when heated, but thermosoftening polymers do?
options: Thermosetting polymers have strong cross-links between the chains; thermosoftening polymers only have weak forces between chains
questions.hint: Think about links between the chains.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The cross-links hold the chains in place.
B: Incorrect — Both are polymers.
C: Incorrect — It is the other way round.
D: Incorrect — Both have polymer chains.

questions.stem: What is a composite material?
options: A matrix (binder) surrounding fibres or fragments of another material that reinforce it
questions.hint: Two materials with different jobs.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is an alloy.
B: Correct — For example, fibreglass or concrete.
C: Incorrect — Composites combine materials.
D: Incorrect — Composites are made of more than one material.

questions.stem: A racing bike frame must be strong and have a low density. Which material is the best choice?
questions.hint: Think about which composite is light and strong.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — It is strong and very light.
B: Incorrect — Glass is brittle.
C: Incorrect — LDPE is light but too weak and flexible.
D: Incorrect — Ceramics are brittle.

questions.stem: What does the Haber process make?
questions.hint: It is used to make fertilisers.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Ethanol is made by fermentation or from ethene.
B: Incorrect — That is made by a different process.
C: Correct — N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
D: Incorrect — Nitric acid is made from ammonia, not by the Haber process.

questions.stem: Where do the raw materials for the Haber process come from?
options: Nitrogen from the air; hydrogen from natural gas
Nitrogen from natural gas; hydrogen from the air
questions.hint: One comes from the air.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Nitrogen comes from the air.
B: Correct — These are purified before use.
C: Incorrect — There is very little hydrogen in the air.
D: Incorrect — Neither comes from sea water.

questions.stem: What conditions are used in the Haber process?
options: About 450 °C, about 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst
Room temperature and pressure, with no catalyst
questions.hint: An iron catalyst, a few hundred °C and a few hundred atmospheres.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — These give a good amount of ammonia at a fast enough rate.
B: Incorrect — Those are fermentation conditions.
C: Incorrect — The temperature is about 450 °C, with iron.
D: Incorrect — The reaction would be far too slow.

questions.stem: How is the ammonia removed from the reaction mixture?
options: The mixture is cooled, and the ammonia liquefies and is removed
questions.hint: Ammonia turns to liquid more easily than N₂ and H₂.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This isn't how it is removed.
B: Incorrect — Ammonia is a gas in the reactor.
C: Incorrect — Burning would destroy it.
D: Correct — N₂ and H₂ stay as gases.

questions.stem: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that don't react?
options: They are released into the air
They are turned into fertiliser directly
They are recycled back into the reactor
questions.hint: Nothing is wasted.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would waste hydrogen.
B: Incorrect — They are recycled.
C: Incorrect — Nitrogen and hydrogen must first become ammonia.
D: Correct — This saves raw materials.

questions.stem: Why is an iron catalyst used in the Haber process?
options: It speeds up the reaction, so ammonia is made faster
It turns the ammonia into fertiliser
It stops the reaction being reversible
questions.hint: Catalysts change how fast.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The catalyst isn't used up.
B: Incorrect — A catalyst isn't used up.
C: Incorrect — That is done in a separate process.
D: Incorrect — The reaction is still reversible.

questions.stem: The forward reaction in the Haber process is exothermic. Why is 450 °C used, rather than a lower temperature?
options: A lower temperature would give a higher yield, but the rate would be too slow, so 450 °C is a compromise
A higher temperature always gives more ammonia
Temperature has no effect on the reaction
questions.hint: Lower temperature: more ammonia, but how fast?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Iron melts at a much higher temperature.
B: Correct — It balances yield against rate.
C: Incorrect — Higher temperature shifts the equilibrium left, lowering yield.
D: Incorrect — Temperature affects both rate and yield.

questions.stem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Why isn't a much higher pressure than 200 atmospheres used?
options: Higher pressure would stop the catalyst working
Higher pressure would lower the yield
Higher pressure would give more ammonia, but the equipment and energy would cost too much and be less safe
Pressure has no effect on the yield
questions.hint: Higher pressure helps, but at a cost.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That isn't the reason.
B: Incorrect — 4 molecules on the left and 2 on the right, so higher pressure raises the yield.
C: Correct — 200 atm balances yield, rate and cost.
D: Incorrect — Pressure shifts the equilibrium here.

questions.stem: A graph shows that the percentage yield of ammonia falls as temperature rises. What does this tell you?
questions.hint: Which direction does heating favour?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Then heating would increase the yield.
B: Correct — Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (backward) reaction.
C: Incorrect — The yield changes, so it is an equilibrium.
D: Incorrect — The yield clearly changes.

questions.stem: A graph shows that the percentage yield of ammonia rises as pressure rises. Why?
options: Higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with more molecules
Higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules, the ammonia side
Higher pressure acts as a catalyst
questions.hint: Count the gas molecules on each side of N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It favours fewer molecules.
B: Incorrect — This isn't the reason.
C: Correct — 4 molecules on the left, 2 on the right.
D: Incorrect — Pressure is a condition, not a catalyst.

questions.stem: Which three elements are in NPK fertilisers?
questions.hint: The letters are chemical symbols.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — K is potassium.
B: Incorrect — N is nitrogen.
C: Correct — N, P and K.
D: Incorrect — N is nitrogen and P is phosphorus.

questions.stem: Why are NPK fertilisers described as formulations?
options: They are mixtures of salts with set percentages of each element
questions.hint: Think about how they are made up.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They contain N, P and K.
B: Incorrect — They are mixtures.
C: Incorrect — They are carefully designed.
D: Correct — The amounts are chosen to suit the crop.

questions.stem: What is ammonia used to make in fertiliser production?
questions.hint: Two things.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Phosphate rock is mined.
B: Incorrect — Glass is made from sand.
C: Incorrect — Potassium chloride is mined.
D: Correct — These are used to make nitrogen fertilisers.

questions.stem: Ammonia reacts with nitric acid. Which fertiliser is made?
questions.hint: Alkali + acid → salt.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — There is no calcium or phosphate.
B: Correct — NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃.
C: Incorrect — There is no potassium.
D: Incorrect — That needs sulfuric acid.

questions.stem: Where do the potassium compounds in NPK fertilisers come from?
options: They are made by the Haber process
Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are mined
They are extracted from the air
questions.hint: They are dug out of the ground.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Crude oil contains hydrocarbons.
B: Incorrect — The Haber process makes ammonia.
C: Correct — They can be used as fertilisers.
D: Incorrect — There is no potassium in the air.

questions.stem: Why can't phosphate rock be used directly as a fertiliser?
options: It is insoluble, so it is treated with acid to make soluble salts
questions.hint: Plants take in nutrients dissolved in water.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Plants can only absorb dissolved salts.
B: Incorrect — It is the main source of phosphorus.
C: Incorrect — It is a rock.

questions.stem: How does making ammonium sulfate in industry differ from making it in a school lab?
options: The lab makes far more than industry
The lab uses the Haber process
Industry makes it on a large scale from raw materials in several stages; the lab makes small amounts from ready-made ammonia solution and sulfuric acid by titration
questions.hint: Think about scale and starting materials.
questions.rationale:
